danny.notes: Your friend since the cul-de-sac. Still lives four streets over.

priya.notes: Your wife. Reads the terms and conditions, which turns out to matter.

hr.notes: Flown in for the day. Has done nine of these before lunch.

billing.notes: Cheerful. Cannot tell you the price and is not permitted to.

clerk.notes: County office. Sympathetic and entirely powerless about the spelling.

adjuster.notes: Insurance. Records the call and reminds you that he is recording it.

nurse.notes: Explains the options for your father, three of which cost more than his house.

nodes.title: Proving who you are, again
nodes.sum: Every institution verifies you separately, none of them trust each other's verification, and each wants a different combination of documents you must locate, copy and produce in person.

nodes.title: The renewal treadmill
nodes.sum: Passport, licence, registration, insurance, membership, subscription, permit. Each has its own cycle and its own portal, so something is always about to lapse and the lapse is always your fault.

nodes.title: Open when you are at work
nodes.sum: Offices, clinics, banks and tradespeople operate during working hours, so accessing them costs annual leave or lost pay.

nodes.title: Hold music, and the person who cannot help you
nodes.sum: Support lines are built around cost per call. The person who answers can read the screen and rarely change what is on it.

nodes.title: The typo that becomes official
nodes.sum: One wrong character in a name, date, address or account number propagates into every system downstream, and correcting it is always harder than making it.

nodes.title: Their mistake, your problem
nodes.sum: Institutions presume their own records are correct. When they are not, discovering it, proving it and fixing it is entirely the work of the person harmed.

nodes.title: Mistaken for someone else
nodes.sum: Matching is fuzzy. A similar name, a shared birth date or a recycled phone number attaches another person's record - debts, fines, medical history - to you, and disproving it is your job.

nodes.title: After the crash
nodes.sum: The collision takes four seconds. What follows is months of insurers, assessors, hire cars, medical appointments and an argument about liability you did not want to have.

nodes.title: The ordinary injury
nodes.sum: A fall, a ladder, a kitchen, a football pitch, ice. The healing is the easy part; the hard part is doing your job and your life at reduced capacity while nobody adjusts anything.

nodes.title: You get ill, and nobody decided it
nodes.sum: Cancer, autoimmune disease, a cardiac event, a neurological condition. No behaviour reliably prevents them, no one is responsible, and the diagnosis reorganises everything around it.

nodes.title: The waiting list
nodes.sum: Where care is rationed by queue rather than price, the wait is assigned to you without negotiation and without a date you can plan around.

nodes.title: The illness generates an invoice
nodes.sum: In systems that bill individuals, a medical event produces a bill nobody quoted in advance, for an amount nobody can state beforehand, from providers you did not choose.

nodes.title: Cover attached to a job
nodes.sum: Where health cover comes through an employer, losing or changing work removes medical care at the same moment it removes income - and staying in a bad job becomes a medical decision.

nodes.title: The body slows on a timetable you do not set
nodes.sum: Recovery lengthens, sleep degrades, eyesight goes, strength declines. Gradual enough to be invisible, cumulative enough to be decisive, entirely non-negotiable.

nodes.title: Being burgled or robbed
nodes.sum: Someone decides to take your things. The loss is the smallest part; the aftermath is locksmiths, insurers, reference numbers, and not feeling right in your own rooms.

nodes.title: On the receiving end of someone else's driving
nodes.sum: Another person's speed, phone or inattention arrives in your life at a junction, and everything that follows is yours to administer.

nodes.title: Where you live decides which disaster you get
nodes.sum: Flood, wildfire, hurricane, earthquake, heatwave, freeze. The exposure comes with the ground, and the ground came with the job, the family or the price.

nodes.title: Someone is trying to defraud you, professionally
nodes.sum: Calls, texts, emails and messages engineered by people who do this full time, arriving whether or not you engage with anything.

nodes.title: Your data was lost by someone you never dealt with
nodes.sum: Organisations you have no relationship with hold records about you and lose them. Nothing you did caused it and nothing you can do fixes it.

nodes.title: The job ends because someone else did arithmetic
nodes.sum: Layoffs, restructures, acquisitions and closures arrive on a timetable set elsewhere. The decision is about headcount and cost centres, not about you, and the income stops anyway.

nodes.title: The manager you were assigned
nodes.sum: Whether a job is tolerable is largely one person, allocated to you, who can change without notice and without any change to your contract.

nodes.title: Working while ill, because the alternative is worse
nodes.sum: Where sick pay is thin or absent, illness becomes a financial calculation, and the calculation usually says go in.

nodes.title: Your largest expense is set annually by someone else
nodes.sum: For renters, the price of having somewhere to live is decided by another party once a year, and the only counter-move costs more than accepting it.

nodes.title: Things break, and they break together
nodes.sum: Boiler, roof, car, washing machine, phone. Each has a lifespan, they were often bought at the same time, and they fail at whatever moment they fail at.

nodes.title: Someone will need looking after
nodes.sum: An ageing parent, a sick partner, a child with additional needs. It arrives unscheduled, lasts years, is unpaid, and lands on whoever is nearest or least able to refuse.

nodes.title: Bereavement, and the paperwork of it
nodes.sum: Grief arrives with an administrative workload - registration, probate, accounts, utilities, pensions - executed by the person least able to concentrate.

nodes.title: Locked out of your own account
nodes.sum: Identity online is a chain of recovery methods. Break one link - a dead number, a lost authenticator, a closed email - and the chain does not reconnect.

nodes.title: The thing you relied on is discontinued
nodes.sum: Services close, formats are abandoned, apps are bought and shut, devices stop receiving updates. The decision is a company's; the migration is yours.

nodes.title: You must have a car, because of how the place was built
nodes.sum: Where there is no viable transit, car ownership is not a preference - it is a condition of employment, imposed by planning decisions made before you arrived.

nodes.title: The commute
nodes.sum: A daily journey is the largest recurring involuntary time cost most working people carry. It is unpaid, not counted as work, and mostly set by where housing is affordable.

nodes.title: The credential you must hold to be considered
nodes.sum: Employers set entry requirements. Roles that once needed a school certificate now need a degree, without a corresponding change in the work - so the qualification is a toll, not a choice.

nodes.title: The structures that made friends are removed
nodes.sum: School, university and early jobs supply repeated unplanned contact. Adult life does not, so friendship becomes something that must be organised or it ends.

nodes.title: You cannot afford to enforce your own rights
nodes.sum: Most everyday legal wrongs are worth less than the cost of pursuing them, so the right exists and the remedy does not - and the other party knows it.

nodes.title: Compelled participation
nodes.sum: Jury service, tax filing, census, registration, court witness summons. Duties that take real time, are not optional, and are scheduled by the state.

nodes.title: Everything you have requires upkeep
nodes.sum: Possessions, accounts, documents, health and qualifications all decay without input. The work returns you to baseline; none of it is progress.

nodes.title: The queue
nodes.sum: Waiting is allocated to you by whoever is providing the thing, in units they do not pay for and you cannot spend elsewhere.

nodes.title: You were born into a cohort and the cohort has a price
nodes.sum: House prices, interest rates, the labour market in your graduation year, whether a pandemic falls in your twenties. None is chosen, and all of it compounds.

nodes.title: The volume of small compulsory decisions
nodes.sum: Tariffs, plans, policies, renewals and options all require comparison. The choosing is imposed; the alternative is paying the default price.

nodes.title: Ambient activation that never resolves
nodes.sum: News, notifications and always-on messaging produce a baseline of alertness nobody opted into, and it does not switch off because the devices do not.

dusk.text: {player}, I'm gonna stay here. Like, on purpose. Is that bad?

options.text: I tell him it isn't.
I say I want to go somewhere.

isnt.text: It is not bad. He will still be four streets over in thirty years and will be, on balance, happier than you.

fourth-of-july-in-a-yard.title: Fourth of July in a yard

start.text: Somebody's yard, a folding table, a cooler, and a grill being operated by a man who will not accept help.
There are neighbours here you see once a year and like a great deal for exactly one afternoon.
Eat something, {player}. You're all bones.

options.text: I eat something.
I ask her about the freezer in the garage.

freezer.text: Because you never know. My mother knew.
Her mother did know. That freezer is a piece of inherited memory, three generations from the thing it remembers.

options.text: I stay out until the end.

stay.text: Nothing about today required a permit, a fee, an appointment or a document.

the-credential-you-must-hold.title: The degree as a filter, and what it costs

start.text: The jobs you want all say 'bachelor's degree required'. Most of them do not need one to do; it is a filter, and filters are cheap for the people applying them.
The degree costs more than your parents' first house. You will borrow most of it, at a rate set by statute, and the debt cannot be discharged in bankruptcy.
I got hired off a handshake and a shop test, {player}. That's gone, huh.

options.text: I sign the loan paperwork.
I ask what happens if it doesn't pay off.

ask.text: Then you still owe it. That's the part they don't say on the tour.

sign.text: You sign. Four years later you have the degree and the debt, and the first job that required the degree does not use it.

options.text: I am glad I went.
I do the arithmetic and regret it.

glad.text: You are glad. Both things are true at once and stay true.

regret.text: The arithmetic is not favourable. Neither is the arithmetic of not having gone, which is the trap.

out.text: Nobody refused you anything. The gate was priced, not guarded.

start.text: You apply for a passport because of a trip. The form is two pages. The fee is about 130 dollars and it comes in five weeks.
There is no interview. Nobody asks your purpose of travel, your employment, your bank balance, or whether you intend to come back.
{player}, that's it? You just... fill it in?

options.text: I say yes, that's it.
I ask what she means.

mean.text: My cousin waited fourteen months for an appointment. To be told no.
You have nothing to say to that, so you say nothing, which is the correct response and feels inadequate.

yes.text: It arrives in five weeks. It is the most powerful document you will ever hold and it took less effort than a parking permit.

out.text: It gets you into most of the world without asking anyone in advance. You will describe this, for the rest of your life, as 'having a passport', as though that were one thing.

the-typo-that-becomes-official.title: One wrong letter, and eleven months

start.text: Your new health insurance card arrives with your name spelled {document} - one letter wrong, entered by somebody at some point and propagated since.
It does not match your driver's licence, so the pharmacy cannot run the claim, so the prescription is 340 dollars instead of 15.
I can see it's wrong. I can't change it here - it comes from the employer feed.

options.text: I ask who can change it.
I ask what I do about the prescription today.

who.text: Payroll sends it to the carrier. So: payroll. Then it cycles at the end of the month.

today.text: Pay it and submit for reimbursement. Keep the receipt.

loop.text: Payroll says the carrier holds it. The carrier says it comes from payroll. Each is describing their own system accurately.

options.text: I call both, on speakerphone, at the same time.
I give up and use the wrong spelling everywhere.

both.text: It takes eleven months and a supervisor who breaks a rule to fix it. Nobody was obstructive. There was simply no one whose job it was.

adopt.text: You start writing {document} on things, because it is faster than being right.

out.text: A clerical error cost you eleven months of small friction and about 600 dollars. In another life the same error would have cost somebody a border crossing.

start.text: A meeting appears in your calendar at 8:40 for 9:00, with a room you have never been in and an HR partner you have never met.
Thanks for coming. I'll get right to it - your role has been eliminated.

options.text: I ask whether it's me or the role.
I ask what the package is.
I say nothing and let the silence sit.

which.text: This is true, and it is also what is said when it is not true, so it carries no information at all.

silence.text: She waits it out. She has done nine of these before lunch and the silence is in the training.

package.text: Ten weeks, and we'll cover COBRA through the end of the quarter.
COBRA is the right to keep your employer's health insurance after you stop working there - by paying the entire premium yourself, which is usually several times what was deducted from your paycheque.

options.text: I ask what the COBRA premium actually is.
I sign the paperwork.

cobra.text: I'd have to look it up. It's usually more than people expect.
It is 1,640 dollars a month for the family.

sign.text: Your badge stops working before you reach the elevator, which is automated and is not personal, and feels extremely personal.
Nobody did anything to you. A spreadsheet somewhere had a number that needed to be lower.

start.text: Appendicitis, at two in the morning, six weeks after the layoff and three weeks after the COBRA payment you decided to skip.
The surgery is routine and successful. You are home in two days.
This is not a bill. Your provider has submitted a claim. You may receive a separate bill.

options.text: I add up the separate bills.
I call and ask for the total.

call.text: I can tell you what we've billed. The surgeon and the anaesthesiologist bill separately - they're not employed by the hospital.
Three organisations, three invoices, one appendix.

add.text: Hospital, surgeon, anaesthesia, pathology, and a facility fee that is a fee for the building having been used.
Thirty-one thousand dollars, of which you owe most, because for three weeks you were a person without coverage.

options.text: I ask for the uninsured rate.
I ask for a payment plan.
I ask what happens if I don't pay.

rate.text: There's a self-pay discount. That brings it to about nineteen.

plan.text: We can do zero percent over twenty-four months.

dont.text: It would go to collections, and that affects your credit.

out.text: You are well. The appendix was removed competently by people who were good at their jobs, and it will take four years to pay for.

cover-attached-to-a-job.title: Why the next job is chosen for you

start.text: Two offers. One is the work you want, at a small firm, no coverage for ninety days.
The other is duller, larger, and the insurance starts on day one. Priya's inhaler is 380 dollars a month without it.
Take the boring one, {player}.

options.text: I ask if she's sure.
I take the boring one.
I argue for the one I want.

sure.text: I'm not sure. I'm just not willing to gamble on it.

argue.text: You argue well. Ninety days is not long. Then you both do the arithmetic on what ninety uncovered days cost last time, and stop arguing.

boring.text: You take the job with the coverage. It is a good job. It is not the job.
Tying health cover to employment means that every career decision for the rest of your life has a medical question underneath it.

start.text: Stationary traffic. You are hit from behind at about forty by a man who was looking at his phone.

options.note: you do not yet know that you are not

options.text: I say I don't know yet.

fine.text: Six weeks later the neck pain is constant. 'No injuries at the scene' is now a recorded statement in your own voice.

dontknow.text: It is the right answer and it feels evasive, which is exactly why most people do not give it.

out.text: The settlement covers the car. The physical therapy is twelve sessions, of which insurance covers eight.
Four seconds of somebody else's attention, and you will feel it in cold weather for the rest of your life.

the-house-and-the-payment.title: Your largest expense, set by somebody else

start.text: You buy the house. Thirty-year mortgage, a rate you did not choose, set by a committee in Washington responding to an economy you are not part of.
Then the escrow letter: property tax reassessment and an insurance premium that has gone up 31% because of wildfire risk four counties away.
Four hundred and ten dollars a month. For the same house.

options.text: I appeal the assessment.
I shop for other insurance.
I absorb it.

appeal.text: You appeal, and win a reduction of eleven dollars a month after four months and two afternoons off work.

shop.text: Two carriers have stopped writing new policies in the state entirely. The third quotes more.

absorb.text: You absorb it, which is what almost everybody does, because the alternative is moving.

out.text: The house is yours in every sense that matters and in no sense at all: the largest number in your life is reset annually by people who will never see it.

you-must-have-a-car.title: Built so that not driving is not an option

start.text: The transmission goes on a Tuesday. The quote is 4,200 dollars, which is more than the car is worth.
Without it you cannot reach work, which is eleven miles away with no bus that runs before seven.

options.text: I ask what the bus would take.
I finance a replacement.

bus.text: Two buses and a walk. Two hours and ten minutes each way, and the last one back leaves before your shift ends.

finance.text: You finance a used car at 14.9%, because the credit report still carries the medical collections.
That's the thing, {player}. Being broke costs more.

options.text: I agree.
I work out what the interest totals.

total.text: Six thousand four hundred dollars for a nine thousand dollar car. The medical debt from four years ago is still charging you rent.

out.text: Nobody required you to own a car. The place was simply built on the assumption that you would, which is the same thing arriving by a different route.

someone-will-need-looking-after.title: Your father, and what the options cost

start.text: Your father has started leaving the stove on. Then it is the front door. Then it is your mother's name, for four seconds, in the middle of a sentence.
There are three options, and I'll be honest with you about what they cost.

options.text: I ask her to be honest.
I ask what Medicare covers.

medicare.text: Medical care, yes. Long-term custodial care - help with washing, dressing, eating - largely no.
The thing most people assume is covered is the specific thing that is not.

options.text: Memory care is between six and nine thousand a month. Home aides are about thirty an hour. Or somebody in the family stops working.
I'll do it, {player}. I'm retired, it's fine.
I say she can't do it alone.
I offer to take two days a week.
I look at whether he qualifies for Medicaid.

alone.text: She will do it alone for fourteen months before she says anything, and by then she will have lost eleven pounds.

twodays.text: Two days a week, which becomes three. Your employer is understanding for about five months.

medicaid.text: He would qualify after spending down almost everything he owns, including the house. The programme is designed that way.

out.text: Nobody in this story is treated unjustly. There is simply a cost, and it lands on whoever in the family is least able to refuse it - which is almost always a woman.

cannot-afford-to-enforce-your-rights.title: Being right, and that not being enough

start.text: The contractor took 14,000 dollars for a roof, did about a third of it, and stopped answering.
You are unambiguously in the right. Every document supports you.
Consultation: $350. Retainer: $3,500. Estimated cost to judgment: $12,000-$18,000.

options.text: I ask about small claims court.
I ask what happens if I win.

small.text: The limit in your state is 10,000 dollars, which is less than you lost, and you would be giving up the rest to use it.

win.text: You get a judgment, which is a piece of paper saying he owes you. Collecting it is a separate process, at your expense, against a man with no assets in his own name.

options.text: I sue anyway.
I take the small claims limit.
I do nothing.

sue.text: You win in fourteen months. You have collected 1,100 dollars of it to date.

take.text: You take the 10,000 cap and write off the rest, which is the rational choice and feels like being robbed twice.

nothing.text: You do nothing, which is what he was relying on, and which is a business model rather than a failure of yours.

out.text: You had every right. Rights are free; using them is not, and the gap between those two facts is where he operates.

the-house-where-the-family-gathers.title: The house where the family gathers

start.text: Thanksgiving. Nineteen people, four of whom are new since last year, in a house that is objectively too small for this.
Same table. I ate at this table when I was nine.

options.text: I ask her what it was like then.
I carry the table outside because it won't fit.

then.text: Crowded. Same as this. That's the good version, {player}.

carry.text: It goes in the yard, under the maple, with an extension cord and two space heaters. It is the best one anybody remembers.

out.text: Your father does not know most of their names now and is perfectly happy, which is a mercy nobody expected.
This is the thing the whole arrangement was for. It is not diminished by what it cost.

a-tree-you-planted.title: A tree you planted that is now large

start.text: The maple was a stick in a plastic pot from a hardware store, planted the spring you moved in, staked with a length of hose so the wire would not cut it.
It is now taller than the house and the whole yard is in its shade by four in the afternoon.

options.text: I sit under it.
I look for the old stake.

stake.text: The hose is still there, grown into the bark about nine feet up, a green ring the tree closed around and carried with it.

sit.text: You complained about digging that hole for a week.

options.text: I say it was a very hard hole.
I admit I don't remember digging it.

hard.text: It was a hard hole, {player}. You were right.

forget.text: You don't. She does, in detail, including what you said about the clay.

out.text: Nobody approved this tree. Nobody had to. It simply got large while you were busy, which is the only way anything does.
